title: He Filed 11 Fake H-1B Petitions, Forged Executive Signatures, and Became an American Citizen. Now the DOJ Wants It Back.
excerpt: Indian-origin CEO Neeraj Sharma is among 17 naturalised citizens targeted in the Trump administration's expanding denaturalization campaign.
body:
The U.S. Department of Justice has filed to revoke the American citizenship of Neeraj Sharma, an Indian-born CEO in New Jersey, as part of a sweeping denaturalization drive that targeted 17 naturalised citizens in a single week.

Sharma's case stands out for its specificity: he ran a staffing company, filed 11 fraudulent H-1B visa petitions, forged executive signatures on corporate letterhead, and then lied about all of it when he applied for citizenship. The government wants it back.

## The Fraud

Sharma, 50, was the owner and chief executive officer of Magnavision LLC, an IT staffing company based in Piscataway, New Jersey. Between 2015 and 2017, according to the Department of Justice, he signed and filed 11 H-1B visa petitions with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. Each petition falsely claimed that the visa beneficiaries would be employed by a major global financial institution.

The petitions included letters on the institution's official letterhead bearing forged signatures of its executives. The positions described in the petitions did not exist.

In 2017, while these fraudulent petitions were on file, Sharma applied for naturalisation. Under penalty of perjury, he told USCIS that he had never committed a crime for which he was not arrested, never provided false information to government officials, and never lied to gain immigration benefits. All three statements, the DOJ alleges, were false.

His application was approved. He became an American citizen in December 2017. He was subsequently convicted of fraud and visa misuse.

## The Denaturalization Campaign

Sharma is one of 17 individuals targeted in the latest batch of denaturalization actions filed across multiple federal districts. The others include a Mexican national convicted of possessing child sexual abuse material, a Dominican convicted of illegal drug distribution, and several others accused of concealing criminal histories during their citizenship applications.

"American citizenship is a privilege, and it must be earned honestly," said DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin. "If you come here, break our laws, and lie in your immigration proceedings, you forfeit that privilege."

The Trump administration has dramatically accelerated the use of denaturalization, a legal tool that was rarely deployed in recent decades. Between 1990 and 2017, federal courts handled an average of 11 such cases per year. During Trump's first term, the pace roughly doubled to 25 annually. In his second term, the Justice Department issued a directive last year instructing its civil rights division to "prioritize and maximally pursue" these proceedings.

In May alone, the DOJ moved to strip citizenship from 12 individuals. The June batch of 17 brings the year's total well above the historical average in just six months.

## Why This Matters Beyond One Man

Sharma's case is a cautionary tale that cuts through the H-1B debate in ways that neither side finds comfortable.

For immigration hawks, it validates the argument that the visa programme is riddled with fraud — that staffing companies file bogus petitions, fabricate job offers, and exploit workers who have no real position waiting for them. The 11 petitions Sharma filed represented 11 people whose immigration status was built on forgeries.

For the Indian tech community, which accounts for roughly 70 per cent of all H-1B visas issued annually, cases like Sharma's are a reputational liability. They feed the narrative that Indian-run staffing firms are uniquely prone to gaming the system, even though the vast majority of H-1B holders work legitimate jobs at companies that compete fiercely for talent.

The case also arrives at a moment when the H-1B programme is under simultaneous legal and legislative assault. A federal judge this week struck down the Trump administration's $100,000 fee on H-1B applications, ruling that only Congress has the power to create such a tax. But Republican lawmakers have already introduced the PROTECT American Workers Act to codify a similar fee through legislation.

## What NRIs Should Know

Denaturalization remains exceedingly rare — the U.S. has naturalised more than 9 million people since 2010, and the number of revocation cases is in the low dozens per year. The legal bar is high: the government must prove that citizenship was obtained through fraud, concealment, or material misrepresentation.

But the current administration has made clear it views denaturalization as a tool to be used aggressively, not sparingly. For naturalised citizens who obtained their status legitimately, the legal risk is negligible. For anyone who concealed criminal conduct or misrepresented facts during the immigration process, the calculus has changed.

A separate lawsuit filed this month by 70 Indian graduates adds another dimension. The graduates are suing the U.S. government over H-1B denials that resulted from their employers' fraud — arguing they should not be punished for deception they did not commit or even know about.

The distinction matters. In the immigration system Sharma exploited, the workers were as much victims as the government was. They came to America with legitimate skills and were placed at companies through fabricated paperwork. When the fraud was uncovered, it was their visas that were revoked, their careers that were disrupted, and their lives that were upended.

Sharma, who profited from the scheme, became a citizen. Until the DOJ came calling.

**Sources**: U.S. Department of Justice, USA Today, Livemint, Storyboard18, Washington Examiner
